Rate movement by vehicle class

Charged rate per $100 of agreed value is the rate-on-line equivalent for this book: gross written premium at 100% divided by the agreed value it insures. Sample size is printed above every bar.

The book softened 14.2% between periods and it softened in every one of the six classes, not in one or two cells that could be an account effect. Median rate fell from 1.498% to 1.285% per $100 of agreed value. The leave-one-out table below tests whether any single account is carrying that movement.

Exposure and premium per policy

Agreed value is the exposure base. If value per policy rises while rate falls, premium per policy can hold flat while rate adequacy deteriorates — these two charts separate those effects.

Terms: catastrophe deductible and vehicle age

Two deductible bases run in the same column: a flat $5,000 and 2% of agreed value subject to a $10,000 minimum. The first chart covers percentage-basis policies only. Basis mix moved 40.4% to 39.4% on the percentage basis.

Green where the movement favours the buyer, red where it favours the carrier. Direction is inverted for deductibles and agreed value, since a higher deductible and a lower insured value both reduce what the carrier is exposed to.

Monthly rate consistency

Solid line is a three-month trailing mean; dashed is the raw monthly median. Points are hollow where the month carries fewer than five bindings, and hollow months are excluded from the rolling calculation.

The rate decline is a steady grind across all twelve months rather than a step change at any single renewal date. That pattern is consistent with market-wide softening rather than with one large account renewing at a materially different price.

Volume and exposure by month

Policy count tests whether the book is growing; median agreed value tests whether the growth is coming from more cars or from more expensive cars.

Terms drift by month

The share of policies written on the percentage-of-value catastrophe deductible. A falling share means the book is absorbing more of each catastrophe loss.

Consistency scorecard

Coefficient of variation across the twelve monthly observations, and the drift implied by a linear fit from first month to last. Under 10% is stable, 10 to 25% shows some variation, above 25% is volatile.

Two checks require the coverholder's attention. Every row in all twelve months carries a zero underwriting judgement adjustment, so charged premium equals technical premium exactly and portfolio rate adequacy is 1.00 book-wide — the field records no underwriter deviation at all, which is either a genuine no-deviation book or a field that is not being populated. Separately, the surplus lines tax rate is empty on all 7,655 rows, so the workbook's own mandatory-field check fails on every row and the tax and stamping columns cannot compute. Both should be resolved before the next syndicate submission.

Hazard tiering here is the carrier's own zone classification, not cat-model output. There is no storm footprint, no site correlation and no modelled PML behind these numbers. 4,095 policies sit in high-hazard zones carrying $2.14B of exposure net to capacity.

Where the premium goes

The 25% ceding commission stack splits evenly between the broker and Torque Underwriters, leaving 75% net to capacity across the ten-syndicate panel.

Hazard concentration by vehicle class

Agreed value stacked by hazard tier within each class. A class weighted toward high-hazard zones needs more rate than the class median suggests.

State accumulation

Bars are net catastrophe exposure to capacity; the overlaid line is that state's share of the book on the right axis. Bars turn amber above 4% of book and red above 8%.

State shares here sum to 100%, and that is a property of this book rather than a normalisation. Every policy garages one vehicle at one address, so no policy is exposed in two states at once and there is no double count to reveal. The largest single-state accumulation is CA at 5.7% of book — a well spread position across 50 states. This is the opposite of the concentration problem a property book usually has, and it is the one number here that would change most if the book grew through a regional producer.

Three exposure measures

There is no single correct number for state exposure. Gross agreed value is the absolute ceiling and assumes a total loss on every car. Net of the catastrophe deductible is what the policy would actually pay on a total loss. Net to capacity applies the panel's 75% share and is the headline figure.

Account spread

Accounts ranked by the number of states their vehicles are garaged in. A multi-state account is diversified against a single event; a single-state account with many cars is not.

550 of 550 accounts garage vehicles in more than one state, and the widest spread reaches 20 states. Single-state accounts carrying several high-value cars are the real single-event accumulation in this book, not the large multi-state portfolios.

The panel is flat and it has not moved. All ten markets sign an identical 10% line, and that split is byte-identical across all twelve monthly submissions — no market has grown or trimmed its participation since August 2025. Every market therefore carries the same $7.13M of gross written premium, the same $401.84M of net catastrophe exposure and the same $213.62M of that exposure in high-hazard zones. Nothing on this tab differentiates one market from another; what it sizes is what each of them is signing up to.

Signed premium by market and period

Split by the two reporting periods. Equal bars are the expected result on a flat panel — an unequal pair would mean a line changed mid-term and the bordereaux did not carry it through.

Premium into the panel by month

Gross written premium at 100% by month of inception. This is the volume the panel is absorbing; each market takes 10% of it. Solid line is a three-month trailing mean; dashed is the raw monthly figure.

Premium into the panel is growing while the rate per $100 of agreed value falls 14.2%. The panel is writing more cars at a lower price, so premium growth here is volume, not rate. Tab 2 separates the two.

Catastrophe exposure by market and hazard tier

Each market's net catastrophe exposure to capacity, split by the zone tier recorded on the certificate. This is what a single market would be reserving against a total loss across the tier.

What one 10% line carries by state

The top twelve state accumulations reduced to a single market's signed share. Hover any bar for the equivalent figure at 100%.

A single 10% line's largest single-state accumulation is $23.05M in CA, against $401.84M of total net catastrophe exposure. No market has more than 5.7% of its exposure in any one state.

Limitations carried forward. The 2025 period covers five months (August to December) against seven for 2026 (January to July); per-month figures are the fair comparison for any growth claim, and the paired bars compare medians rather than totals for that reason. All 7,655 rows are new business bound within authority, so nothing here measures renewal retention or renewal rate change. Every row prices at technical premium with a zero judgement adjustment, so this dashboard measures the movement of the technical rating basis, not underwriter deviation from it. Hazard tiering is the carrier's own zone classification, not CatNet or cat-model output: no storm footprint, no cross-site correlation, no modelled PML. The source workbooks are marked synthetic demo data.
